text: Section five. Principle five: Handlers only set the next state. Computing a class instead of adding one. In plain JavaScript, we change the look of an element by adding or removing a CSS class. Here is a small example. A picture should get a blue frame when the user clicks it. Our style sheet has a class for that, picture dash dash active. The plain way finds the picture element by its ID and keeps it in a variable called image. Then it adds the class on the click. Three short lines of plain JavaScript in picture.js. Line one tells image to listen for a click with add event listener. Line two is the whole point. On the click, image.className.add puts in the class picture dash dash active, and the note on that line says it plainly, a command, put the blue frame on this element. Line three just closes it up. React does not ask us to command the element. Instead, we compute the class name from state on every render. In the React version, this is picture.jsx. Line one imports useState from React. Line four gives us a piece of state, is active with its setter, set is active, and it starts as false. Then line six makes a variable, class name, holding the string picture. Lines seven and eight say if is active is true, add a space and picture dash dash active to the end of it. The note there says exactly that. Add the second class to the text when is active is true. And line eleven returns an image. Its class name is the one we just worked out, the class text computed above, as the note puts it. On click, it calls set is active with true. The source is park.jpg, and the alt text is the new park. The sign plus equals comes from JavaScript. Used on a string, it adds text to the end of it. So when is active is true, the text grows to picture space picture dash dash active, and the space at the start of that second part keeps the two class names apart. The user clicks the picture once. The elements panel then shows both classes on the image. Look at figure twenty-four. It's the elements panel after that one click. There's the image tag, and its class attribute holds both names, picture and picture dash dash active. Its alt is the new park, and its source is park.jpg. The note beside it says both classes were computed from is active. React wrote them both into the class attribute. Here is what happened in order. One click, and the handler set is active to true. Then React drew picture again. This time, is active was true, so the class name became picture space picture dash dash active. And last, React compared the new class name with the old one, which was just picture. They differ, so React wrote the new class name into the image's class attribute. The handler never talks about classes. It only says that the picture is now active. The React docs describe the rule like this. In React, you need to describe what you want to see rather than manipulate the UI elements. This is the taxi again. The handler names the address, and React drives. Now, connecting the handler to the form. Now we finish the promo code box. The handler from principle three goes inside the component below the success check. It also needs check code, so the file imports it from our fake server. Here's the top half of promo code.jsx in the components folder. Line one imports useState. Line two brings in check code from checkCode.js one folder up. Inside the component, line five holds the code starting as an empty string. Line six holds status starting as the string typing. Lines eight to ten are the success check. If status is success, we return just one paragraph. Code applied. You get free delivery. And then from line twelve, the handler. Handle submit is async, and it takes the event, e. Line thirteen calls preventDefault on it. Line fourteen sets status to checking, and the note says, Next look, checking. Then a try. Line sixteen awaits check code with our code. If that works, line seventeen sets status to success. Next look, success. And if it fails, the catch sets status to error on line nineteen. Next look, error. The handler does nothing else to the page. It does not turn the box off. It does not show checking. It does not hide the error line. It only names the next look. The form gets the handler through on submit. The box also gets a class that is computed from status, so it has a red border in the error look. The rest of the same file is the part it returns. Line twenty-four opens the form with on submit set to handle submit. The note says, Apply sends the form, and React calls handle submit. Line twenty-five is the heading, promo code. Then the input from line twenty-six. Its class name is a ternary. If status is error, it's code box and code box dash dash error. Otherwise, just code box. The note says, Red border only in the error look. Its value is code. On change, it calls setCode with the typed text, e.target.value, and it's disabled when status is checking. Line thirty-two is the button. It's disabled when the code is empty or when status is checking. Its word is apply. Then two short lines. Line thirty-five shows a checking paragraph only when status is checking with the double ampersand. And line thirty-six shows a paragraph with the class error saying, This code is not valid, only when status is error. The ternary on the box works like the one in light. In the error look, the box gets two classes, code box and code box dash dash error. In every other look, it gets only code box. The style sheet holds the classes that both versions of the page use. Three rules in index.css. Hidden gets display none, error gets color red, and code box dash dash error gets a border two pixels solid red.
